An uncertain nuclear effects model

P(missy) is a nuclear effects model that carries its uncertainty instead of rounding it off. The numbers these calculations run on are ranges in their own sources and single values by the time they reach a conclusion. This one keeps them as ranges, all the way through, and computes what the weapon burns as well as what it destroys. Madeline Berzak

Hi! I’m Madeline, but everyone calls me Maddie. I’m based in Chicago, where I lead the nuclear risk research program at the University of Chicago Existential Risk Lab.

p(missy) came out of what I can only describe as a very large mind map: two years of small insights and loose threads from conversations, finally pinned to one page. What I kept noticing was that nuclear winter never enters the conversation about targeting, and that the parameters the field runs on come from a book published in 1977. Blast physics has not changed. What has changed is how much we know about everything downstream of it, and we still flatten complex systems and uncertain ranges into single point estimates that leave most of that complexity out. I think that pushes the field away from the longer-term consequences of nuclear risk, nuclear winter among them.

I built p(missy) because uncertainty belongs in the conversation, and because nothing existed that made it legible to experts and non-experts at once.

Enjoy it, and tell me what you think. I am always after feedback, at mberzak@uchicago.edu.

– Maddie <3

About (missy)

Every input to a targeting calculation is a range, not a number.

P(missy) is an uncertain nuclear effects model. Rather than solving the standard targeting math once with every input fixed at a single value, it evaluates that same math right across the range each input actually occupies, so that what comes back is a spread of answers rather than one.

The parameters it models are the familiar ones, lethal radius, SSPK, p(miss) and p(kill), and they are the numbers behind force posture analysis, research on weapons effects, and much of what is understood about operational planning. They are what an analyst reaches for in asking whether a counterforce strike could work, how much of an arsenal would survive one, and what an exchange of that kind would cost in lives. P(missy) does not alter any of those formulas; what it shows is how much of the resulting answer was decided by assumptions rather than by physics, which is something a single number can never disclose.

Those inputs are also far less settled than they appear. A hardened silo sits somewhere between 1,500 and 5,000 psi depending on which silo and whose estimate you take, wartime reliability is somewhere above 0.8 and nobody who says so can tell you where above, and accuracy is a design specification rather than a measurement of anything that has ever been done in anger. The convention is to take a value from the middle of each of those ranges and carry it forward as though it had been settled all along.

Carrying the ranges instead moves the answer, and it moves in one direction only, because the chance of a miss is raised to the number of warheads assigned to each target, which means that averaging across a range will always leave more silos standing than running the middle of that range does. The gap widens as the ranges widen, and it falls on precisely the question counterforce analysis exists to answer, which is whether the other side would have anything left to retaliate with.

A second argument runs underneath all of this. The fight over counterforce and countervalue targeting is conducted almost entirely on the fallout ledger, counting who dies downwind of a silo field, while fire is the mechanism that actually puts soot in the stratosphere, and nobody adds the two ledgers on the same page. I think the risk of a nuclear winter belongs inside targeting calculations. It isn't in them yet.

What current models miss

What the models we use actually account for.

This is not a complaint that models are simplified, since every model is, and simplifying is most of what makes one usable. The claim is narrower than that. The three tools the field relies on take almost entirely disjoint sets of inputs, and not one of them carries uncertainty from one stage through to the next. Most of the terms in the lower block of the table appear in none of them at all, and two of those rows are empty for p(missy) as well, along with a third for height of burst, which has no closed form available to borrow. Every cell here can be checked against the tools themselves, which is why this is a table rather than an argument.

Push yield and height of burst down and fallout casualties fall dramatically, which is the standard counterforce result and the reason planners reach for small, accurate weapons rather than large ones. Those same two settings also govern the thermal pulse, and with it how much of the ground below catches fire, so one of these ledgers is counted with real care while the other is not counted at all.

The Effects of Nuclear Weapons

Our understanding is built on a book from 1977.

Samuel Glasstone and Philip Dolan compiled The Effects of Nuclear Weapons for the Departments of Defense and Energy, and the third edition from 1977 has been the reference for blast physics and thermal dynamics ever since. Most of p(missy)'s numbers come out of it. The field still uses many of the visual graphs in Glasstone and Dolan to determine the optimal height of burst (how high to detonate a nuclear weapon) that achieves a certain amount of overpressure to properly destroy a target.

It is a dense book and it is still the one the field runs on. What it cannot account for is everything downstream of the blast that has changed since 1977, which is where the uncertainty in the nuclear winter chain actually lives.

The physical processes have not changed. What goes wrong is downstream of them, when an assumption hardens into doctrine and a range is carried forward as a single standardised data point. Three of those are below.

Three assumptions

Each one is a range the field collapsed into a single number. Click on a panel to open an assumption.

Atmospheric transmittance is the fraction of the thermal pulse that survives the trip to the target: how much light gets through the air without being absorbed or scattered out of the beam. How far the pulse reaches therefore depends on whether the day is clear, overcast, humid, hazy, foggy or raining. That distance sets the radius of the circle inside which things catch fire, and that circle, taken with how much combustible material is standing in it, is what the estimates of how much burns and whether a firestorm forms are built on.

While Glasstone and Dolan acknowledge that atmospheric transmittance varies greatly, for the purposes of their calculations they assume it is equal to 1.0: a very sunny, perfectly clear day. Their own figures put transmittance at about 0.9 on a clear day, 0.6 on a hazy one with moderate visibility, and 0.3 in fog or rain. Go from the clear day to the fog and the ignition area falls by 67%, which is two thirds of the fuel a nuclear winter estimate is counting. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and other aerosols also absorb selectively by wavelength, so transmittance is not one number for the whole pulse; it is a function of the spectrum. The equation, and where its constant comes from, is written out on the model page under Fire.

Glasstone and Dolan brush past this assumption completely, and as a result, the field also brushes past this today.

The ignition threshold is the amount of heat a material has to absorb before it catches fire, measured as thermal fluence in calories per square centimeter. In other words, how much energy has to land on a surface before that surface starts burning? Glasstone and Dolan put the working figure at about 10 cal/cm², and that single number is what sets the ignition radius. For a 15 kiloton airburst like Hiroshima, 10 cal/cm² is reached about 2.03 kilometers out, which gives an ignition area of roughly 13 km². Every estimate built on the Hiroshima proxy starts from that circle. But the book's own tables run from 4 cal/cm² for shredded newspaper up to 50 for new bond typing paper, so the number carried forward is one value taken out of a range spanning more than a factor of ten.

There is a second problem, which is that the threshold is not a property of the material alone. It also depends on how fast the heat arrives. A fixed threshold assumes the energy is delivered instantaneously, and it is not: the thermal pulse of a 1 kiloton airburst lasts about 0.4 seconds, while a 10 megaton explosion takes more than 20 seconds to deliver its energy. Slower delivery gives heat time to conduct away before the surface reaches ignition temperature, so thick wood, wet materials and dense plastics all need more energy from a big weapon than they would from a small one. Glasstone and Dolan say as much themselves. The threshold rises with yield, and the models built on their work still use one number for every weapon.

Bigger weapons also shade themselves. In a 20 second pulse, the fires that start in the first five seconds put up smoke that shields the edge of the target area for the remaining fifteen, and surface bursts loft enough debris to cut the fluence arriving further out by 20 to 40% compared to a cleaner airburst. A static circle is being used to describe something that unfolds over time.

Fuel load is a term the nuclear field uses to encompass the amount of combustible material within a given target area. In other words, what could and will burn, and at what rate? Think about how cities are constructed today, versus how they were constructed in the mid-twentieth century. Hiroshima, at the time of the atomic bombing in 1945, was constructed almost entirely of wood with no more than two floors in a building. It was also confined to a clearer geographic area, unlike the vast urban sprawl of modern cities, where skyscrapers gradually melt into crowded suburbs, parks and industrial corridors. Modern cities like New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles tower with skyscrapers and dense city-centers constructed predominantly with reinforced concrete, structural steel and plate glass. We also need to think about the presence of plastics, as well as the interior contents of buildings that will also be subject to ignition.

A target list and relative nuclear winter risk constructed upon 1940s urban morphology is making an implicit bet about the atmosphere, and that bet belongs inside the targeting calculation rather than downstream of it. Which way the bet runs is not settled either. Concrete and steel are harder to set alight than the wood of 1945, while the plastics inside them give off two to three times more soot per unit mass than wood does, and those two facts pull in opposite directions.

Ignition radius at three transmittances · 15 kt airburst
Excellent visibility, clear day τ ≈ 0.9 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.9 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.94 km area = π(1.94)² ≈ 11.8 km²
Moderate visibility, hazy τ ≈ 0.6 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.6 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.58 km area = π(1.58)² ≈ 7.8 km²
Poor visibility, fog or rain τ ≈ 0.3 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.3 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.12 km area = π(1.12)² ≈ 3.9 km²

f is the thermal fraction of yield, Y the yield in calories, Q the ignition threshold in cal/cm², and τ the atmospheric transmittance: the fraction of the light that survives the trip, which is what visibility measures. Between clear air and fog the ignited area falls by 67%, which is where that figure comes from. The equation for τ itself, and where its constant comes from, is written out on the model page under Fire.

How to use the model

The model reproduces a worked example, and then you widen it.

It opens on a case taken out of a targeting briefing: a W78 warhead at 335 kilotons and 120 metre accuracy, aimed at a silo hardened to 3,000 psi, two warheads to each silo and two hundred silos in the set. Run it as it stands and it returns the figures the briefing does. The Checks tab tests every one of them against results already in print, every time the page loads, and says so plainly if any of them drift.

Where to start

  1. Open One target and read the steps from the top down. That column is the standard method, taken apart: a lethal radius, a damage function, where the warhead lands, and the chance the target survives what is aimed at it. The last row is the number a briefing reports.
  2. Look at the three figures above the steps. The first is the chance one warhead kills the target, the second is the chance the target survives all of them, and the third is what happens to the second once every input is allowed the range its own sources give it. The distance between the second and the third is what the model exists to show.
  3. Now pick a different target and a different weapon from the two menus at the top of the panel. Each one sets a value and a span, both taken from the source named beside it. A weapon is not a number; it is a number with a footnote, and the footnote is what changes the answer.
  4. Widen a span by hand. Every control on the panel carries one: a value on the slider and a range underneath it in the same unit. Take hardness across the full 1,500 to 5,000 psi a silo can occupy and run it again. Nothing about the physics has changed. Only the honesty about the inputs has.
  5. Go to Equations, not one equation, which does the same thing to the formula itself rather than to what is fed into it. Untick two of the lethal radius expressions so only one is in play, run it, and put them all back. The gap between those two runs is the part of the answer that comes from nothing but a choice of published equation.
  6. Move to Target set, where the same answer is carried out to a field. Read What each input is worth first: it sorts the inputs by how far each one moves the answer on its own, and that ordering is usually the most useful thing on the page.

What each input means

The panel is the equation. Its groups are the groups in p(kill; target | weapon | delivery | environment), in that order, and every control on it is one named term. Five terms carry a label saying named, not computed: those are the ones this model can name but does not evaluate, and they are on the panel rather than left off it so that the size of the omission stays visible.

Hardness, H
The blast overpressure a target absorbs before it stops working, in pounds per square inch. A silo is 1,500 to 5,000; a road-mobile launcher is 2 to 5, and so is an ordinary house.
Damage function width, σD
How fast the chance of destroying the target falls off across the lethal radius. At 0 it is the cookie cutter every published formula assumes. At 0.20 it is the Sigma-20 curve Davis and Schilling name and then decline to use.
Footprint, A
Zero for a silo, which is a point. Not zero for an apron, a garrison or a dispersal area, where a warhead landing anywhere on the footprint is on top of the target. This is the term that lets the model leave silos.
Yield, Y
The energy released, in kilotons. Hiroshima was about 15, and the W78 on a Minuteman III is 335. The same yield drives the fire calculation on the third tab.
Warheads on this target, n
The exponent. Assign more than one and the target survives only if every one of them misses, which is where the whole convexity argument comes from.
Height of burst
Only the Brode and Small pressure field reads it. Leave it above zero and switch formulas to watch three of the four stop responding to an input that matters.
CEP
A containment radius: draw a circle of this radius on the aim point and half the warheads land inside it. It is a 50% localisation region, not a one-sigma figure and not a bound. The familiar 68% belongs to one axis at a time; the circle of radius one σ holds about 39%, and it takes about 1.3 CEP to reach 70%.
Shape of the error, σdr/σcr
The C in CEP stands for circular and the real error is an ellipse, longer along the line of flight than across it. This is the ratio of the two, with CEP held fixed as it moves. Nothing in the open literature gives this ratio for a deployed system, which is exactly why it is a control here rather than a buried assumption.
Aiming bias, b
A systematic offset of the whole pattern from the target: guidance calibration, accumulated gravity model error, or a target whose surveyed coordinates are wrong. Unlike CEP it does not average out over many shots or over many targets, which is why it is carried separately.
Reliability, ρ
The share of warheads that arrive and go off. Cold War testing points to something above 0.8 for advanced arsenals, which is a floor rather than a number.
Fratricide, q
The chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead aimed at the same target. Arrivals are seconds apart and debris persists, so the first two are unaffected and the risk starts at the third. At 0 it is the independent case every published formula assumes.
Targets in the set, N
How many targets are being attacked. Two hundred is roughly a silo field. Set it to 1 to read the calculation for a single target, with no counting at all.
Yield exponent
How lethal radius scales with yield. Every formula here uses the cube root, 0.3333, which follows from peak overpressure alone. A silo is damaged by how long the pressure lasts as well as how high it climbs, and a bigger weapon holds it longer, so cube-root scaling understates a megaton-class warhead. Working back from Wohlstetter's own figures gives 0.3690, anchored at 50 kt.
Lethal radius formula
Which published expression the steps use. It is set to the General Electric calculator, the one the standard exchange arithmetic inherited, so the single answer stays comparable to what a briefing reports.
Formulas the quadrature draws from
Which expressions the ranges are carried across. Davis and Schilling print four readings of lethal radius, all fitted to the same test data, and at five megatons against a 300 psi target they return anything from 3,762 to 4,095 feet. That disagreement is an uncertainty like any other, and there is no reason it should be the one input a model treats as settled.
Points
How finely the box of input ranges is covered. There is no seed and no run-to-run variation: the point set is a lattice, so the same inputs give the same answer every time. The convergence line reports what the last doubling moved.

What comes back

Inputs as set
One pass with every input fixed where its slider sits. This is the number a briefing reports, and it is the thing the rest of the page is measured against.
Spread from chance alone
What you get if the odds themselves were known exactly and only the coin was uncertain. This is the error bar usually quoted alongside a result, and it is the smaller of the two.
Spread once the ranges are carried
The average across the whole box of input ranges, with a 95% band. Nearly always the largest of the three, and always on the same side of the single answer.
What each input is worth
One bar per input, each running from the answer at one end of that input's range to the answer at the other, so the longest bar is the input the answer depends on most. The values printed under the ends of a bar are the input values that produce them, which is where the direction is legible. The ticks inside a bar are at equal steps of the input, so evenly spaced ticks mean an even trade and bunched ticks mean the middle of that range is not a fair summary of it.
One hundred attacks
A hundred outcomes read off the distribution at even intervals, stacked over the number of targets each one left standing. They are read off rather than drawn, so nothing in the picture clusters by accident.
Worth holding on toOne target here means one aim point rather than one warhead, and a surviving silo may hold a MIRVed missile carrying several of them, so the number of surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs in the same direction as the convexity gap does, which is toward understating what the other side would have left to retaliate with.

Carrying the uncertainty

The method was invented for this exact problem, in the same laboratory.

The idea is to answer a question you cannot pin the numbers down for. Rather than solving the problem once with a single value for each input, you solve it over and over across the range each input could plausibly occupy. What happens to the answer if the accuracy is a little worse, the silo a little harder, the weather a little foggier? What comes back is not an answer but a distribution of answers, and the shape of that distribution is exactly what a single calculation cannot tell you.

The method and the subject grew up together. Stanislaw Ulam arrived at the modern version of it at Los Alamos in 1946, while recovering from an illness and playing solitaire. He wanted to know the odds that a hand of Canfield would come out, found the combinatorics tedious, and realized he could lay out a hundred hands and count the wins instead. The problem he actually needed it for was neutron diffusion in a weapon core, which had plenty of data and no way to be solved on paper. John von Neumann carried the idea to the ENIAC, Nicholas Metropolis supplied the name, and the first fully automated Monte Carlo calculation, in the spring of 1948, was of a fission core.

Castle Bravo is what it looks like when a range gets collapsed into a single number. Detonated at Bikini Atoll on 1 March 1954, it was predicted at 6 megatons and delivered 15. The predicted range was really 4 to 8 megatons, and some of the designers had cautioned that the yield could reach 15, but 6 was the figure that traveled. The error underneath it was one assumption: the lithium-7 in the fuel, about 60% of the lithium content, was treated as inert, and it was not. It produced tritium instead, and that tritium fused. The largest weapon the United States has ever detonated came in at two and a half times its design yield, eight years after Monte Carlo was invented in the same laboratory, because one number in the calculation was carried forward as though it were settled.

So the case for carrying a range rather than assuming a value is neither new nor abstract. What is strange is that the targeting math downstream of the weapon never took the method up. Force posture analysis is still done overwhelmingly at the middle of every range and reported as a single figure, even though the tool for doing otherwise was built in the same place, for the same reason, and is now cheap enough to run in a browser tab.

Why it suits this problem

  1. The math is cheap. One pass through lethal radius, SSPK, reliability and p(miss) takes a fraction of a millisecond, so a few thousand passes take well under a second. There was never a computational reason to avoid doing this, only a question of patience.
  2. Averaging the inputs is not the same as averaging the answers. p(miss) raised to the number of warheads is a convex function, which means the answer taken from the middle of every range sits systematically below the average of the answers across those ranges. Carrying the range is the only way to see that gap, and no amount of care with a single calculation will reveal it.
  3. What is worth reporting is a distribution. Anyone who needs to know the risk that twenty silos survive rather than one is asking about the tail of a curve, and a point estimate does not have a tail.

Why this model no longer rolls dice

Everything above is an argument for carrying the range. It is not an argument for drawing random numbers, and version 5 of this model stopped doing that.

Look at what is actually being asked for. The average of p(kill) across a set of input ranges is an integral over a box: six or eight dimensions wide, with a smooth integrand and known edges. Pseudorandom sampling is a way of doing that integral, and by modern standards a poor one. Its error falls as one over the square root of the number of draws, it clusters and leaves gaps because that is what random numbers do, and it makes the answer depend on a seed, so a result cannot be quoted without quoting the seed alongside it.

What this model uses instead is a rank-1 lattice: a deterministic point set spread evenly through the box by construction, generated from the plastic constant in as many dimensions as there are ranges. On this integrand its error runs about ten times below pseudorandom sampling at the same number of points, and that is checked on the Checks tab rather than asserted here. There is no seed. There is no run-to-run variation. Two people who set the same inputs get the same answer to the last digit printed, which for a method meant to audit other people's numbers is not a nicety.

The change is also worth making for what it says. A simulation invites the reading that the model is generating scenarios, rolling for outcomes, playing the war out. It is not, and it never was. It is evaluating one function across the range of inputs the literature actually supports and reporting the range of answers that come out. Calling that quadrature rather than simulation is the more accurate description of what is happening, and the more honest one about how much is being claimed.

Two things follow from it on the page. The counting that happens after the integral — how many of two hundred targets survive, given the odds for one — is closed form and is not approximated at all, so the band reported around it is exact rather than sampled. And a field of targets with different hardnesses is now spread evenly across its span rather than drawn from it, which is why nothing in the figures clusters by chance any more. It used to, and the clustering looked like it meant something.

What it does not doNone of this invents information. If the ranges going in are wrong, the distribution coming out is wrong with more decimal places attached. The method carries uncertainty through a calculation; it does not reduce it. Every range in the panel is a judgment, taken from the open literature where the literature has one, and marked in gold where it does not.

Where to read more

  1. Eckhardt, Roger. “Stan Ulam, John von Neumann, and the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 131–41. mcnp.lanl.gov.

    • The origin story, the solitaire hand, and von Neumann's letter proposing the ENIAC calculation. Also the clearest short explanation of what a random number generator has to do, and why that is harder than it sounds.

  2. Metropolis, Nicholas. “The Beginning of the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 125–30.

    • The companion piece, by the man who named the method, on how it was actually run on the machines of the late 1940s.

  3. Metropolis, Nicholas, and S. Ulam. “The Monte Carlo Method.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44, no. 247 (1949): 335–41. doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1949.10483310.

    • The first unclassified paper on the method and the first to carry the name. Six pages, and readable.

  4. National Security Archive. “Castle BRAVO at 70: The Worst Nuclear Test in U.S. History.” Briefing Book, February 29, 2024. nsarchive.gwu.edu.

    • The declassified record behind the yield figures above, including the General Advisory Committee minutes giving the predicted yield as four to eight megatons, and Carson Mark's explanation that lithium-7 had been assumed to be a much less good fuel than lithium-6.

Case study

Auditing a published counterforce estimate against its own footnotes.

This is the tab the written case study will live in. It applies the model to Lieber and Press, The New Era of Counterforce (2017), and it is being finished separately; what follows is the shape of the argument and the numbers the model returns, so that the method can be read here even before the essay is.

The audit, in four moves

  1. Reproduce. Their Table 1 reports 42, 13 and 8 surviving silos out of 200, for the 1985 Minuteman III, the 2017 Minuteman III and the Trident II carrying the W88. Setting the model to the assumptions the paper states returns 42, 13 and 8. That is the precondition for everything after it, and it is checked on every page load under Checks.
  2. Widen, using their own footnotes. Not ranges invented for the purpose — the ranges the paper itself cites for accuracy and for silo hardness. The headline numbers do not move. A band appears around them where there was none.
  3. Read the asymmetry. The low-yield option is far more sensitive to that band than the high-yield one. The probability that at least one target survives rises several-fold for the first and barely at all for the second, which means the two options are not comparably robust even where they report comparable means.
  4. Name what is outside the frame. The humanitarian case for counterforce in this literature is argued on a fallout ledger. Fire is absent from the arithmetic, and it is the mechanism that drives the nuclear winter risk. The two ledgers have never been added on the same page, which is what the Fire tab is for.
On footnote 53The footnote where fire is excluded from the calculation is the same footnote that cites Lynn Eden's book on how fire came to be excluded from targeting doctrine in the first place. That is the editorial centre of the essay, and the reason this model computes both ledgers from one set of inputs rather than treating the second as somebody else's field.

Nothing in the audit says the published numbers are wrong. Run the model at the assumptions the paper states and it agrees with the paper. What the audit says is that a single number was the wrong shape of answer to the question being asked, and that the range the authors themselves supply is enough to change what follows from it about force structure.

FAQs and applications

FAQs and Applications

p(missy) is an instrument for testing whether other people’s answers survive their own admitted uncertainty.

Research applications

Audit checks of published research

Taking any counterforce result, for instance Lieber and Press’s survivor counts, Philippe and Stepanov’s fallout casualties, or the LLNL study group’s force-sizing logic, and asking whether the conclusion holds when the inputs are given the ranges their own sources publish. p(missy) is an instrument for doing exactly that.

The two-peer problem and force sizing debates

The core question is how many warheads are needed for two peers. That argument runs downstream of exchange arithmetic evaluated at point estimates. If the honest output is a distribution, then the requirement is a distribution too.

The question becomes how many warheads are needed to achieve what confidence of what outcome. That is a different question and a far more scrutable one. Uncertainty can mean you need more warheads, or it can mean the mission is unachievable at any number. Convexity pushes toward the second.

Prioritizing measurement

p(missy) can tell you which unknowns are buying the most spread.

If reliability drives 60% of the output variance and yield drives 4%, then the next research dollar goes to reliability. That is a Sobol decomposition, it is a small amount of work on top of what the model already does, and it converts p(missy) from a critique into a research agenda.

So, what changes?

Any published counterforce result can now be checked against the ranges its own sources admit to. Force sizing stops being a number and becomes a confidence level, which is a much harder question to hand-wave. And you can see which unknown is buying the most spread, so you know where the next research dollar goes. That last one is not built yet, though it is an afternoon of work.

Does anything like this exist?

Not for exchange calculations. The sensitivity analysis tradition exists, and Kent and Thaler were doing something adjacent in 1989, but running the standard targeting chain over its own admitted input ranges and reporting the distribution is not in the open literature.

Frequently asked

Is this a targeting tool?

No. It reproduces published counterforce formulas in order to show how much of their output is decided by assumptions rather than by physics. Nothing in it is operational, and every formula in it is already in print.

Where do the numbers come from?

The blast and thermal formulas are from Glasstone and Dolan (1977). The lethal radius expressions, and the disagreement between them, are from Davis and Schilling (1973). The worked example the presets reproduce is from Lieber and Press (2017). Full citations are under Sources.

Why does widening the ranges only ever leave more targets standing?

Because the chance of a miss is raised to the number of warheads assigned to each target, and that function is convex, so the average across a range always exceeds the value at the middle of it. The effect is one-directional by construction rather than by any choice of parameters.

Can I reproduce a result?

Yes, and there is nothing to remember in order to do it. Nothing on the model page is random: the ranges are integrated over a fixed lattice of points rather than sampled, so there is no seed and no run-to-run variation. Set the same inputs and the same numbers come back, to the last digit printed. Every setting and every point travels in the exported CSV.

Why is fire treated separately from blast?

Because the field treats it separately, which is the argument. The Fire tab runs from the same yield and the same burst height as the exchange calculation on the first two tabs, and no existing open tool reports both from one set of inputs.

Is any of this classified?

No. Every formula, table and figure used here is from the open literature, and each one is cited under Sources.

Eleven things this is built out of.

  1. Acton, James M. “Two Myths about Counterforce.” War on the Rocks, November 6, 2023. warontherocks.com.

Equation 37 gives peak overpressure from a surface burst as 3300Y/r³ + 192√Y/r3/2 in psi, with the yield in megatons and the range in kilofeet, and inverting that is what their lethal radius fit approximates rather than derives.
    • §Air Blast for the two qualifications the fits drop: equation 38 for the decay behind the shock front, and the overpressure impulse, which is the quantity a buried silo actually responds to. Brode is explicit that peak overpressure alone is the wrong variable for a hardened structure, which is the physical content of the pulse duration correction carried as a range on the model page.

  4. Brode, Harold L., Dale A. Larson, Richard D. Small, Stephen J. Speicher, and Frank J. Thomas. Fire, Airblast, and Underground Effects from Nuclear Explosions—Some Current Progress. DNA 5741T. Santa Monica, CA: Pacific-Sierra Research Corporation, 1981.

It is the only expression on this page that can see height of burst at all; the four in Davis and Schilling are surface-burst readings with height already assumed away.
    • The appendix prints forty-seven scaled range and height pairs with the resulting overpressure to four decimal places. Twelve of them run under Checking the math, which is why the implementation here can be trusted rather than asserted.
    • Used to test the claim on p.212 of Davis and Schilling that for silo hardnesses a surface burst does more damage than an air burst. Against this pressure field that holds at 300 psi and fails above it: the best height against 3,000 psi reaches about 9% further than a surface burst, and about 13% further against 5,000 psi.

  5. Davis, Lynn E., and Warner R. Schilling. “All You Ever Wanted to Know about MIRV and ICBM Calculations but Were Not Cleared to Ask.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 17, no. 2 (June 1973).

Pages 211 to 214 print the reading off the AEC graph, the Greenwood and Brode expression both full and truncated, and the General Electric Missile Effectiveness Calculator, together with the single shot kill probability each one implies for the same weapon against the same target. Note 11 supplies the 0.369 yield exponent that corrects for pulse duration. Note 12 supplies the Sigma-20 damage function, and it is the most useful thing in the article: it prints three points off the curve and the kill probability the curve produces, then declines to use any of them. Fitting those three points recovers a normal curve in radius whose standard deviation is 20% of the lethal radius, which is what the name means and which this model now runs. The article also records that the two corrections pull opposite ways and roughly cancel for its own weapons, so carrying one without the other, as every open-source tool built on these formulas does, is the one choice here that is not defensible in either direction.

(missy)

A nuclear effects model that carries its uncertainty instead of rounding it off. The same inputs that set the odds of destroying a target also set how far the weapon starts fires, and both are computed here from one set of numbers.

Inputs

Equations, not one equation

Davis and Schilling print four readings of the same test data, entry 05 under Sources, and the four do not agree. The fifth is not a reading of hardness at all: it evaluates the pressure field and finds where it crosses the target hardness, so height of burst becomes an input instead of an assumption
Which formula to believe is itself an open question, so it is carried as one more dimension of the integral. Untick all four and the formula chosen above is used alone

Precisionhow carefully the ranges are covered, not what the answer says

NPoints across the ranges 4,096
—
This is the only control on the panel that does not change the answer. It changes how carefully the answer is worked out. The model has to average p(kill) over every combination of the ranges you have opened, and it does that by evaluating the calculation at this many points spread evenly through them. More points cost time and buy accuracy you cannot see at the digits printed; fewer are quicker and eventually start to wobble. 4,096 is the default because that is where the answer stops moving. The points are a fixed lattice rather than a random sample, so there is no seed: open this page tomorrow with the same settings and the same digits come back

What each input is worth

One bar per input. Each runs from the answer you get at one end of that input's range to the answer at the other, so the longest bar is the input your answer depends on most. The values under the ends of a bar are the input values that produce them, which is where the direction is: more accuracy pushes one way, a harder target the other. The ticks inside a bar are at equal steps of the input, so evenly spaced ticks mean an even trade and bunched ticks mean the middle of that range is not a fair summary of it.

Using this in research

The model is small on purpose. What it is for is taking a number somebody has published and asking what happens to it when the inputs are given as the ranges the sources themselves print.

  1. Reproduce the published number first. Set the controls to the assumptions the paper states and check the model returns its headline figure. The Lieber and Press rows under Checks are that test: their Table 1 gives 42, 13 and 8 surviving silos and this page returns 42, 13 and 8. If it does not reproduce, stop; nothing after this means anything.

  2. Widen each input to the span its own source gives. Not a span you invented — the one in the footnote. The published number will not move. A band will appear around it where there was none, and that band is the result.

  3. Read which input the band is made of. The bars under What each input is worth sort the inputs by how far each one moves the answer on its own. That ordering says which measurement would be worth arguing about and which would not, and it is usually not the one the literature argues about.

  4. Ask the planner's question, not the analyst's. The number a force-sizing argument needs is not the average. It is the chance that nothing survives, which is on the chart above and cannot be recovered from a mean and an error bar.

  5. Export and cite. The CSV carries every quadrature point and every setting. The point set is deterministic, so a result quoted from this page can be reproduced exactly by anyone who sets the same inputs.

Not yet, but nextA target list rather than a target count: a file with one row per aim point carrying its own hardness and footprint, and then the allocation problem, which is how to spread a fixed number of warheads across a fixed set of targets. After that, population and casualty figures, which is the same arithmetic reading a different column. Both are the reason this model is built around one target first.

The three equations behind that number

Daniel asked to see these written out rather than described, so here they are, in the form Glasstone and Dolan give them.

1 Q(d) = f · Y4πd² · τ(d)

Radiant exposure at distance d, in calories per square centimetre. f is the fraction of the yield Y emitted as thermal radiation, and 4πd² is the surface of the sphere that energy has spread over by the time it arrives. G&D §7.101–7.102. Everything except τ is geometry.

2 τ(d) = exp(−3.912 · d / (V · B))

Atmospheric transmittance is the fraction of that energy that survives the trip. Air scatters and absorbs light, and how much it does is what visibility measures: V is defined as the distance at which transmittance falls to 2%, and ln(0.02) = −3.912, which is where the constant comes from and is the whole of the derivation. So at one visibility distance 2% of the light is left, at half of it about 14%, at a quarter about 37%. B is a buildup factor: the plain exponential counts only light that reaches the target without being deflected once, and light scattered forward out of the beam still arrives and still ignites, so the effective path is longer than the geometric one. G&D handles this with the curves at Fig. 7.42–7.43 rather than with a coefficient, and B here stands in for them. It is the one number on this tab with no measured basis, which is why it is marked.

3 Q(R) = Qign(material, Y)  →  solve for R

The ignition radius is the distance at which the exposure delivered equals the exposure that material needs. Qign is read from the tables below and depends on the yield as well as the material, because a larger weapon delivers the same energy over a longer pulse and more of it is lost to the surroundings while it arrives. There is no closed form for R once τ is in the way, so it is found numerically.

Glasstone and Dolan, Tables 7.35 and 7.40

Radiant exposure required for ignition, in calories per square centimetre, for materials exposed to a burst of the yield at the head of each column. Table 7.35 gives the thresholds themselves. Table 7.40 is the reason there are three columns rather than one: it is where G&D record that the threshold rises with yield, because the pulse from a larger weapon is longer and more heat is conducted away from the surface while it is still being delivered. Between the three tabulated yields this model interpolates on the logarithm of the yield, and below 35 kt and above 20 Mt it holds the end column rather than extrapolating.

Material 35 kt1.4 Mt20 Mt

What the tables do not give. The mix of these materials in a real city. Any uncertainty on the values themselves, which §7.36 calls "somewhat approximate" without saying by how much. Yields between the three columns. And any link at all from an ignition to a fire that spreads. That last gap is the largest one: nine pages on incendiary effects against 151 on blast.

Checked against what is in print

Every time this page loads it runs the calculation against figures already published, carried past the digit a briefing rounds them to. Each block names the entry under Sources it is read from, so any row can be checked against the page it came from. Figures are carried in whatever unit their source printed, which is why metres, nautical miles and feet all turn up in one table, and it is why the model converts on the page rather than inside the arithmetic. If one of these rows says fail, something is wrong and nothing else here should be trusted.

What p(kill) is a function of

The published expressions take a handful of inputs. The list of things that actually bear on whether a warhead destroys a target is longer, and the difference between the two lists is most of what this model is about. Below is the whole list, grouped as it is grouped on the input panel, with what each term does and whether this page computes it.

On the five marked "named, not computed"Leaving a term out is a choice, and a choice that gets buried stops being visible as one. Each of the five is listed with what it would do to the answer, so that the size of the omission is on the page even though the term is not. They fail for three different reasons, which is worth separating. Burial geometry and terrain have no numeric basis anywhere in the open literature that I have found, and that absence is itself a finding. Transmittance and weather are computed, but on the Fire tab, and they do not feed back into the blast calculation because nothing published says how they should. The fuze reliability is the odd one out: it is perfectly well defined and it would change nothing here, because separating the fuze from the delivery chain only matters once reprogramming is modelled, and reprogramming is not. It is listed so that the reason it is absent is a stated reason rather than an oversight.
Every symbol on this page

The names, the units they are carried in, and in a few cases the thing the name hides.

Y kt
Yield. Every Davis and Schilling formula wants megatons, so 335 kt enters as 0.335. Brode and Small scale on kt1/3 and take kilotons directly.
H psi
Target hardness: the peak overpressure at which the target is counted as destroyed. 1,500 to 5,000 psi for a hardened silo, 2 to 5 psi for a launcher or a house.
LR m
Lethal radius. The distance out to which the weapon produces the overpressure the target is rated to withstand.
A m
Target footprint, as an equivalent radius. Zero for a silo, which is a point. Not zero for an apron, a garrison or a dispersal area, where a warhead that lands anywhere on the footprint is on top of the target, so A comes off the miss distance before the damage function sees it. Under a cookie cutter that is the same as adding A to the lethal radius; with a damage function it is not, because the falloff belongs to the weapon and has no business widening with the apron.
CEP m
Circular error probable. The radius of the circle, centred on the aim point, that contains half the warheads. It is a median miss distance and a 50% containment radius, and it is neither a one-sigma figure nor a bound.
σdr, σcr m
Standard deviation of the impact point along the line of flight and across it. Equal only if the error really is circular. The pair is fixed by requiring that half the warheads land inside a circle of radius CEP, which is what CEP means. The familiar shortcut CEP ≈ 0.5887(σdr + σcr) is exact when the two are equal and drifts by about 2% by four to one, so the model solves the containment radius rather than using the shortcut.
b m
Bias: a systematic offset of the whole pattern from the target, from guidance calibration or from an error in the target's surveyed coordinates. Unlike CEP it does not average out over many shots, which is why it is carried separately.
σD dimensionless
Width of the damage function as a fraction of LR. 0 is the cookie cutter, 0.20 is Sigma-20.
ρ dimensionless
Overall reliability: the chance a warhead assigned to a target arrives and goes off. The product of the delivery chain and the fuze.
ρf dimensionless
The fuze's own share of that. Carried separately because a missile lost in boost and a warhead that arrives and duds are the same for the arithmetic here and different for anything that models reprogramming or fratricide.
q dimensionless
Fratricide: the chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead aimed at the same target. Zero is the independent case every published formula assumes.
n, N counts
Warheads on one target, lower case. Targets in the set, upper case.
HOB m
Height of burst. Read only by Brode and Small; the other three have it assumed away at zero.
Every formula on this page

The lethal radius is the one quantity here with more than one published expression, and they do not agree. All of them are below, written as their sources write them, with what each is stated to be good for.

Where 2.62 comes from: it is not derived. Davis and Schilling take it off the General Electric Missile Effectiveness Calculator, a circular slide rule whose scale was fitted to Brode's 1960 test-shot data, and it is the branch of that fit stated for hardnesses above 1,000 psi. The other three coefficients on the panel are the other branches of the same slide rule.

The damage function

D(r) = Φ( (LR − r) / σDLR ). The chance the target is destroyed given a burst at distance r. At σD = 0 it is a step, which is the cookie cutter every lethal radius formula above assumes: certain death inside LR, untouched outside. At 0.20 it is the Sigma-20 function Davis and Schilling name in note 12 and then decline to use. Fitting the three points they print recovers a normal curve in radius with a standard deviation of 20% of the radius, which is what the name means.

Single shot probability of kill

SSPK = ∬ D(r) · g(r) dr, where g is the density of the miss distance. With a circular error and no bias g is Rayleigh with σ = CEP/1.1774 and the integral collapses, at σD = 0, to 1 − 0.5(LR/CEP)² exactly, which is the form Davis and Schilling print. With an elliptical error or a bias, g is the radial density of a displaced anisotropic normal and the integral is done numerically. Nothing has been replaced here, only extended: set the shape to 1:1 and the bias to zero and the published form is recovered to nine decimal places, which is one of the rows under Checks.

What CEP is, and is not

CEP is a containment radius. Draw a circle of that radius on the aim point and half of the warheads land inside it. That is the entire definition: a 50% localisation region, not a one-sigma figure and not a bound.

The confusion worth naming is with the familiar 68%. That figure belongs to one axis at a time, not to a circle. Under circular normal error CEP = 1.1774 σ, so the circle of radius one σ holds about 39% of shots, the circle of radius 1.1774 σ holds 50% by construction, and it takes a radius of about 1.55 σ — roughly 1.3 CEP — to reach 70%. About 21% of shots land beyond 1.5 CEP and about 2% beyond 2.4 CEP. That tail is doing real work here, because a target survives on the tail.

One more thing the C hides. The real error is an ellipse: warheads scatter further along the line of flight than across it, so the 50% region is longer than it is wide. Collapsing it to a circle is close enough when the target is small against the miss distance and wrong when it is not. Nothing in the open literature gives the ratio of the two axes for a deployed system, so rather than invent one the model makes it an input. CEP is held fixed as the shape changes: the two standard deviations are solved so that half the warheads still land inside a circle of the stated radius. Moving the control therefore redistributes a published accuracy figure rather than replacing it, and what you read off is the price of the assumption on its own.

From one warhead to n

TKP = SSPK · ρ, and with independent arrivals a target survives only if every warhead misses, so p(survive) = (1 − TKP)n. That exponent is why the middle of a range and the average across it give different answers, and why they always differ in the same direction. With fratricide switched on the arrivals are no longer independent and the product is taken term by term instead. Given p(survive), the number of survivors in a set of N is binomial and closed form; given a distribution over p(survive) it is that binomial averaged over the distribution, which is also closed form.

Why there is no Monte Carlo here

The question the ranges pose is an integral: average p(kill) over a box of inputs nobody knows exactly. An integral over a box of six to eleven dimensions is a quadrature problem, and drawing pseudorandom numbers is one of the worse ways to solve it — it converges as 1/√N and it makes the answer depend on a seed. This page uses a rank-1 lattice instead: a deterministic, evenly spread point set. On the six spans the defaults carry, measured against a reference run of 262,144 points, its error at 4,096 points is about twelve times below the average error of pseudorandom sets of the same size. That advantage narrows as more ranges are opened and is gone by the time all ten are open at once, which is a known property of lattices built this way and is worth saying rather than glossing over; even there the lattice is no worse than sampling, and it still has no seed. The checks tab tests the point set itself — that it is identical on two calls, that it is equidistributed in every dimension, that it integrates a known integral, and that doubling the points does not move the answer — rather than repeating the comparison, which is too slow to run on every page load. The counting that follows the integral is closed form and is not approximated at all.

This matters beyond tidiness. A simulation invites the reading that the model is generating scenarios. It is not. It is evaluating one function over the range of inputs the literature actually supports, and reporting the range of answers that come out.

Fratricide

Warheads aimed at one target arrive three to five seconds apart, and a burst throws up debris that persists for six to eight seconds, so a warhead is at risk from its own side only once one has gone off ahead of it with time to spare, which is from the third arrival onward. Writing q for the chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead, a warhead two or more places behind a burst arrives with probability ρ(1 − q) rather than ρ.

The arrivals are then not independent, so p(survive) is not a product of per-warhead terms: a warhead is at risk only if an earlier one actually went off, and that same earlier burst had its own shot at the target. Conditioning on which warhead arrives first removes the dependence, because after that every later warhead faces the same debris, and summing over that first index is exact. At q = 0 it collapses to (1 − TKP)n, which is one of the rows under Checks. Lieber, Press and Chipman put q near 0.75.

It is the one correction on this page that runs against the attacker rather than for him, which is why it is worth having next to the ones that run the other way. It is also the crudest thing here: the timings say the immediately preceding burst is the dangerous one, and this treats every burst two or more places back as equally dangerous with no decay. What the problem really wants is a timing model rather than a coefficient.

What is computed, and what is assumed

Worth keeping straight, because the two get confused and only one of them is a result.

Computed

The lethal radius, from the yield and the target hardness. The chance one warhead kills the target, from that radius, the accuracy, the shape of the error and any bias. The chance the target survives n warheads, with or without fratricide. The number of survivors across a field, and the whole distribution of possible numbers including the chance that none survive. All of it from the formulas on this tab, with no fitting and no free parameters.

Assumed

That every warhead aimed at a target arrives independently, unless fratricide is switched on. That the attacker does not re-fire at targets he can see he missed, which he would, and which would raise his result. That the target's failure mode is peak overpressure alone, when a buried structure can also be reached through the soil. That weather is the same everywhere. Each of these is a choice, and the ones that push in the attacker's favour are listed below so nobody has to guess which way the model leans.

What these formulas do not do

Scaffold, not a finding. Parameters marked with a gold mark have no measured basis. One target here is one aim point, not one warhead: a surviving silo may hold a MIRVed missile carrying several, so surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs the same direction the convexity does, toward understating what is left to retaliate with.

Davis and Schilling record that two corrections pull opposite ways and, for the weapons in their own example, roughly cancel: the pulse duration adjustment raises kill probability and the damage function lowers it. Both are on this page, the first as the yield exponent and the second as σD, so that pair is no longer half-counted. What is still missing runs the other way. Reprogramming, which Davis and Schilling model in detail, is not here, and it raises kill probability by letting the attacker replace the missiles he watches fail. Neither is height of burst optimised: the checks show that against a 3,000 psi silo the best burst height reaches about 9% further than the surface burst every formula here assumes, and further still as the target gets harder. An attacker who optimises height does better than this page reports.

On the fire side, transmittance is Beer–Lambert on visibility with a scatter buildup term standing in for G&D Fig. 7.42–7.43. Ignition thresholds are log-interpolated on yield between the three tabulated columns. Not included: secondary ignitions from blast damage, smoke shielding the pulse from what is behind it, terrain and structure shielding in three dimensions, fire spread, fallout.

And the largest one of all, which is not a missing coefficient but a missing connection: nothing here turns a count of ignitions into a fire, or a fire into soot in the stratosphere. That chain is where the nuclear winter literature begins and where the targeting literature has already stopped.

By Madeline Berzak
